clue.text: Crazy MAGA ran America as a repeated crime, for instance

definitions.text: America as a repeated crime, for instance

indicators.note: Crazy means out of its right mind, and letters out of their right mind will not stay in the order the clue prints them.

parts.note: the seven letters of MAGA RAN, re-sorted

explanation.walkthrough: Brendan's theme is the crossword itself, and this clue is where it starts. Watch the definition: it hands you a specimen rather than a synonym, which is what 'for instance' is quietly warning you about.
explanation.definitionFit: AMERICA rearranges into A CRIME with the A used twice, so the phrase does not describe the answer, it is an example of one.

clue.text: Something solvers may lack — and so were not finished

indicators.note: A word left not finished stops short of its last letter, and all three little words in front of this one stop short.

parts.note: 'and' with its tail lopped off
'so' unfinished is down to a single letter
'were' gives up its final E the same way

explanation.walkthrough: The instruction sits at the end and reaches back over three words at once, which is easy to miss: 'and so were not finished' reads as ordinary grammar rather than as three separate amputations.
explanation.definitionFit: What a stuck solver is short of is exactly this, the word that belongs in the grid, so the definition names it by the gap it leaves.

clue.text: Part of bloomer in Guardian? There you have it

indicators.note: Read this one literally rather than as joinery: it says the word sits inside the letters that follow.

parts.note: the answer runs unbroken across the question mark, straddling the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' is doing two jobs at once: a howler in the surface, at the paper's own expense, and a flower in the definition. Only one of them is true.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloomer is a plant that blooms, and the anther is the pollen-bearing head of its stamen, so the definition picks out one organ of a flower.

clue.text: Happens to meet — as any intersecting answer here does

definitions.meaning: the everyday idiom for bumping into somebody you were not looking for

definitions.text: as any intersecting answer here does
definitions.meaning: this is a down entry, so everything that cuts through it is an across one

explanation.walkthrough: The dash is the split, and the second half is a set of directions: look at the grid and check what the entries cutting through this one are called.
explanation.definitionFit: Running across someone is the idiom for a chance encounter, and an entry crossing this one goes left to right, which is what running across a grid means.

clue.text: Good lesson as example of double definition
Traumatized son held by uncle outside

indicators.note: 'Outside' is a position, not a place: the pawnbroker's phrase goes round the other piece rather than beside it.

parts.note: 'uncle' is old slang for a pawnbroker, so whatever he is holding is in hock
S is the family-tree abbreviation for son

explanation.walkthrough: The uncle is the giveaway: an ordinary relative in the surface, a pawnbroker in the parse. That sense of the word survives almost nowhere outside crosswords and Victorian novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Medicine's shock is the body's collapse after injury, so somebody in shock is somebody the trauma has floored.

clue.text: About negative introduction, admission of meanie who delivers jabs?

parts.note: an admission opens with I am, shortened, and the apostrophe is dropped on the way in

indicators.note: 'About' is placing here, not topic: the piece named next ends up wrapped inside what the rest of the clue builds.

parts.note: a meanie is a miser, the one who will not part with a penny
UN- is the syllable English puts on the front of a word to negate it, and it lands just after the M of MISER

explanation.walkthrough: 'Jabs' is the trap: boxing on the surface, vaccination underneath, and the meanie owning up is doing wordplay rather than character work.
explanation.definitionFit: A jab is British informal for a vaccination rather than a punch, so the person handing them out is the one making you immune.

clue.text: Get across what's central to crossword? Separate out valuable bits

indicators.note: It asks for the letter standing at the exact midpoint of the word that follows, not for anything the word means.

parts.note: nine letters, and the fifth of them is the one in the middle
to pan is to wash river gravel until only the gold is left

explanation.walkthrough: A four-letter answer with the theme word supplying just one letter of it: 'crossword' is here to be measured, not to be read.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridge spans a gap, reaching from one bank to the other, which is the same job as getting across it.

clue.text: Excel on course in skill, not in approach

parts.note: whatever is not in is out, the plainest opposition English has
the drive is a house's approach, the gravel sweep from the gate to the door

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the clue sound like golf, which is what makes the seam hard to see: the definition is the golfing sense and the wordplay is a suburban front garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Golf's verb for sending the ball further off the tee than your opponent, beating them at driving, the one skill a tee shot tests.

clue.text: In part of Florida, wife or daughter located crucial elements

indicators.note: The clue opens with its container instruction: everything built afterwards goes inside the place named right here.

parts.note: the Keys are the island chain trailing off the state's southern tip

indicators.note: 'Located' asks where a thing sits rather than what it means, so these letters are being placed in a gap, not defined.

parts.note: W is the genealogist's shorthand for wife
taken at face value: the two letters of the word itself
D is the matching shorthand for daughter, and W-OR-D drops in ahead of the final S

explanation.walkthrough: The joinery word 'or' is fodder, not grammar, and that is the step people miss here: a wife or a daughter reads as a choice rather than as letters to write down.
explanation.definitionFit: A keyword is the one that unlocks a search or a text, 'key' carrying its adjectival sense of crucial rather than naming a piece of metal.

clue.text: Compose crosswords at home to become established

parts.note: the person who composes them is a setter, and what a setter does is set
IN is the standard crossword reading of 'at home': you are in when you are there

explanation.walkthrough: Brendan is describing his own job in the first three letters, which is the sort of joke this puzzle keeps making.
explanation.definitionFit: Of weather, rot or a habit, to set in is to arrive and stay: 'the rain has set in' means it has taken hold for good.

clue.text: River plant may spread in profusion

indicators.note: Something spread has been scattered loose over an area, and letters scattered like that do not come back in the order they left.

parts.note: R is the map's abbreviation for river, and it joins the fodder as a single letter
eight more letters, taken exactly as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: 'River plant' looks like one thing growing in water, and the setter has cut it in half: the river is a letter, the plant is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A weed growing rampantly is growing unchecked and everywhere at once, which is what growing in profusion describes.

clue.text: Closely observing vote in favour, with subsequent outcry heard

indicators.note: 'Subsequent' means coming afterwards, so this piece is added on the end rather than wrapped round anything.
'Heard' hands the clue to the ear: write down what the words sound like, not how a dictionary spells them.

parts.note: a vote in favour is an aye, and an aye said out loud is the organ you see with
an outcry is bawling, and bawling said out loud spells the rest

explanation.walkthrough: One 'heard' at the very end licenses both soundalikes at once, which is why nothing in the middle of the clue looks like an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To eyeball something is to look it over hard and at close range, the informal verb for staring at a thing to size it up.

clue.text: … is 21 reversed? So it is!

indicators.note: The clue wants the other entry written the other way along the row, its last letter first.

parts.note: 21 across is the monster; turn its four letters round and this is what stands there

explanation.walkthrough: The row of dots runs the sentence on from the clue before, so the number is not a number: it stands for whatever 21 turned out to be. The exclamation then cheers the discovery and defines the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergo is the Latin 'therefore' that English kept for mock-formal argument, doing the same job as a conversational 'so'.

clue.text: Builds lead in constituency, embraced by Tory supporters

indicators.note: A word's lead is the letter at its head, so 'constituency' is being asked for its initial and nothing else.

parts.note: a Tory is a Conservative, CON on election night

indicators.note: An embrace closes round whatever it holds, so that letter finishes up inside the other pieces rather than beside them.

parts.note: struts are the supports that hold a structure up
its leading letter, dropped in between the U and the T

explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface is an election night and none of it is politics underneath: 'supporters' means scaffolding, and a lead is a letter rather than a margin.
explanation.definitionFit: To construct is to build, the formal verb a report reaches for where speech would say 'put up'.

clue.text: Kind of setter one's figured out? Produced solution again

parts.note: a red setter is a breed of dog, so a kind of setter is a colour
one is I in crosswords, and the 's comes along as S
to figure something out is to solve it

explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface belongs to crosswords and none of it means what it seems: the setter is a dog and the solution is chemistry.
explanation.definitionFit: A chemist's solution is a solid taken into liquid, so producing one again is dissolving the stuff a second time.

clue.text: Doctor's beginning new round, confused and extremely distant

indicators.note: Something confused has lost track of its proper order, which is what these letters are being told to do.
A word's beginning is its opening letter, so the doctor contributes one character and no more.

parts.note: the first letter of the word Doctor, not the abbreviation DR
eight more letters, taken exactly as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a doctor starting his ward round, which is precisely the wrong picture: nothing here is medical and the letters are all that matter.
explanation.definitionFit: From Britain, Australia and New Zealand sit at the far side of the globe, and Down Under is the nickname that says so.

clue.text: Wordplay known to Greeks, Socratic sort

indicators.note: On the surface 'sort' is a kind of thing; as a verb it means to put into a different order, and that is the job it is doing.

parts.note: the philosopher's adjective, its eight letters re-sorted

explanation.walkthrough: The philosopher supplies the letters and his countrymen supply the definition, so the whole clue stays inside ancient Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is Greek itself, and Greek poets were writing verses whose initials spell out a name centuries before crosswords existed.

clue.text: Little Women, for example, in half a reel?

definitions.meaning: Alcott's March sisters, Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy, come as a set of four, and 'for example' flags a definition by instance
the Scottish eightsome reel takes eight dancers; halve it and the dance is named for the number left

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves point at the number four without ever printing it, one through a novel and one through a dance floor.
explanation.definitionFit: The March sisters are four, so the title names the answer by instance; and the foursome reel really is the eightsome reel halved.

clue.text: Angry outburst about small fight

indicators.note: 'About' puts one piece round another, so the size letter is swallowed rather than tacked on the end.

parts.note: cross is the everyday British word for angry
S is the label sewn into the small size
to have words with somebody is to have a row, so an outburst is words

explanation.walkthrough: This is where the theme surfaces: an angry exchange is cross words, and one extra letter turns the puzzle you are solving into a duel.
explanation.definitionFit: From duelling, where the blades literally cross, the phrase has come to mean clashing with somebody in argument.

clue.text: Like certain answers in relation to clues, some of which I'd denigrate

definitions.text: Like certain answers in relation to clues

indicators.note: 'Some of' wants a piece of the words that follow rather than their meaning, a run of letters lifted straight out.

parts.note: the answer runs unbroken across the tail of the first word and on through the next two

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is doing to this clue exactly what it describes, which is Brendan's favourite kind of joke and worth watching for elsewhere in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidden-word answer lies concealed inside the clue's own letters, so the word describes the relation between that answer and the text carrying it.

clue.text: Girl's name forming part of solution

parts.note: whatever forms part of a thing is in it
a newspaper prints tomorrow's solution as a filled-in diagram, so the solution and the grid are the same picture

explanation.walkthrough: The name says where it lives. Brendan's puzzle is full of clues about crosswords, and this one quietly describes its own position on the page.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a Scandinavian first name, familiar in Britain through Ingrid Bergman, so the clue defines it by category rather than by meaning.

clue.text: Turn back on monster

indicators.note: Going back along a row means reading it right to left, so the piece in front of the word is written the other way.

parts.note: a turn is a GO, as in whose turn is it, and this one is taken backwards
RE means 'on the subject of', the 'on' at the head of a memo

explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn back on' reads as one idiom about rejection. The parse ignores the idiom completely and takes each of the three words on its own, which is the lesson worth keeping.
explanation.definitionFit: The man-eating giant of fairy tale, and by extension anybody brutish enough to frighten children.

clue.text: Nothing in numbers is changed as result of moving 15

indicators.note: Letters told they are changed have to come out different from the way they went in, and their order is the only thing about them that can differ.

parts.note: nothing is a nought, and a nought is written O
nine more letters, taken exactly as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing in numbers' is a single idea on the surface and two separate lots of letters underneath. The cross-reference is the second joke: 15 is a place, and this is what happens when you go there.
explanation.definitionFit: 15 down is DOWN UNDER, and to move down under water is to be submerged, which is exactly what this noun names.

clue.text: Way to address lady in Mother's Union

indicators.note: A union is a joining, so the two pieces are simply written one against the other with nothing done to either.

parts.note: MA is the nursery shortening of mother
a dam is a mother too, the breeder's word for the female parent of a foal or a calf

explanation.walkthrough: The Mothers' Union is a real Anglican society, which is what the surface is counting on. Underneath, 'mother' is asked for twice and answered two different ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Madam is the polite form of address to a woman, the female counterpart of 'sir' and the one a shop assistant still uses.

clue.text: Endure like this clue

definitions.meaning: the verb for something that keeps going without giving out, like a battery
run down the numbering, and nothing follows 24 in the down list

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition points off the page at the clue's own position, so the only way to check it is to look at where the clue is printed.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Endure' is the verb, as in a thing that lasts goes on, while the adjective describes the final item in a series, which is where 24 down sits.

clue.text: Like the most one can do, in terms of manual employment

definitions.text: Like the most one can do, in terms of manual employment

parts.note: The surface pushes 'the best effort somebody can manage', a phrase about trying hard.
The setter means it as arithmetic. 'Manual' is Latin for of-the-hand, so what is being counted is how many of those a person has to put to work, and the maximum is not large.

explanation.walkthrough: There is nothing to take apart here, no fodder and no letters to move. The whole clue is one definition told slant, and the joke is that the limit it describes is a limit everybody already has.
explanation.definitionFit: Working with both hands is the most manual employment anybody can manage, so the phrase for using both is also the phrase for the maximum.

clue.text: Program's producer, person able to handle Morse, say

definitions.meaning: software is written in code, so this names whoever writes it

definitions.text: person able to handle Morse, say
definitions.meaning: Morse is a code, and 'say' flags it as one example of the class

explanation.walkthrough: Morse arrives capitalised and looks like the Oxford detective, which is the whole misdirection: the other reading is the inventor and the alphabet named after him.
explanation.definitionFit: Both halves rest on the noun 'code': software is written in one, Morse is another, and whoever handles either is a coder.

clue.text: Rector having letter forwarded? It's about one name for God

indicators.note: A letter that is forwarded is sent on ahead, so one character leaves its place in the churchman's title and goes to the front of the queue.
'About' is positional here rather than approximate: the six letters close round the single letter that follows.

parts.note: send the C of RECTOR to the front and this is what is left standing
A is the indefinite article, crossword shorthand for one

explanation.walkthrough: Ecclesiastical from top to bottom, a rector and his post and the being he works for, and only the middle of it is doing any wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Genesis has him make the world, so 'the Creator' is the standard reverent title in English for whoever did the making.

clue.text: Solidly constructed — one's mad to change it

indicators.note: To change something is to leave it other than you found it, and the only thing that can differ about these seven letters is their order.

parts.note: the seven letters of ONE'S MAD, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: The dash does the work of an equals sign, and the surface, that you would be mad to change it, is itself the instruction to change it.
explanation.definitionFit: A mason works in stone, and stonework is the byword for building that will not budge, so masoned walls are solidly built.
